items.title: Reasoning about counterfactual choices and responsibility judgements in children
items.author: Fiery Cushman
items.content: Adults judge responsibility by considering not just what someone chose to do, but also the alternative choices available to them. In this Review, Gautam and Cushman consider three processes involved in children’s understanding of counterfactual choices and their relation to responsibility judgements.

items.title: The role of long-term memory, flexible templates and learning in attentional guidance
items.author: Geoffrey F. Woodman
items.content: Theories of visual search suggest that humans hold a veridical representation of the desired target in working memory to guide attention. In this Review, Carlisle and Woodman synthesize evidence that attentional guidance is flexible, adaptive on the basis of experience, and driven by multiple coordinated mechanisms.

items.title: From sample diversity to interpretive convergence
items.author: Taro Murakami
items.content: Generative artificial intelligence tools are being increasingly used by scientists, especially as writing aids for researchers outside English-dominant institutions. However, these tools might narrow interpretations even when applied to increasingly diverse samples. Sampling diversity will not be enough to broaden behavioural science if interpretive diversity is lost.

items.title: Empathy as a dyadic process
items.author: Anat Perry
items.content: Empathy frequently arises in interactions between two people rather than within a single individual in isolation. In this Review, Genzer and Perry consider the cognitive, affective and motivational aspects of empathy through a dyadic lens that considers the empathizer, the recipient and their shared experience.
